title: Trump Readies Fresh Tariffs on Dozens of Countries as India Pushes Back on Forced Labor Duties
excerpt: The temporary 10% global tariff expires Friday, and the administration is investigating about 60 countries under Section 301 for forced-labor violations. India has formally asked the USTR to reconsider a proposed 12.5% levy.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump administration plans new tariffs as the temporary 10% global tariff expires soon.
  • India and 47 countries face potential 12.5% duties over forced-labor allegations.
  • India argues against tariffs, claiming insufficient evidence for forced-labor violations.
  • A bilateral trade deal between India and the U.S. is ready but awaiting timing.
  • Brazil is the first country hit by new Section 301 tariffs, facing 25% duties.

The Trump administration is poised to unleash fresh tariffs on dozens of countries as soon as this week, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, as the temporary 10% global tariff introduced in February is set to expire on Friday.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer confirmed the administration is preparing new trade actions. "We expect to see some action soon," Greer told CNBC on Tuesday. "I can't really specify a timeline right now."

The developments come at a critical moment for India, which faces potential tariffs on two separate fronts while simultaneously negotiating a bilateral trade deal with Washington.

The Expiring Global Tariff

The current 10% tariff was imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broader global tariff policy in February. That section allows temporary tariffs for up to 150 days to address balance-of-payments concerns.

According to the FT report, the most immediate new duties are expected to match the existing 10% rate. Imports from 14 countries and the European Union could face a 10% tariff, while 45 other countries, including China, could face 12.5% duties.

The administration is also pursuing other legal avenues, including investigations under Section 301, that could give it authority to impose higher tariffs with stronger legal footing.

India Pushed Back on Forced Labor Tariffs

In a separate but related action, the USTR launched Section 301 investigations in March examining 60 economies over concerns linked to forced labor and excess industrial capacity. On June 3, it proposed fresh tariffs on 54 economies, with India, China, and 46 others facing a steeper 12.5% duty.

India has formally rejected the allegations. In a submission to the USTR on July 6, New Delhi argued that the agency had failed to identify any specific unfair trade practice that would qualify as "unreasonable" under the law.

"A mere absence of a forced labour import prohibition cannot be construed as 'unreasonable' within the meaning of Section 301 of the Act."

— India's submission to the USTR, July 6, 2023

India further argued that the USTR had not met the evidentiary threshold required to show how the absence of forced-labor import bans meaningfully distorts market conditions. New Delhi said it remains willing to engage constructively through consultation and dialogue.

India-US Trade Deal in Limbo

The tariff pressure comes even as both governments have publicly struck a positive tone on bilateral trade negotiations. India's Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal said on July 13 that a framework deal is ready and both sides are waiting for the right timing to sign.

"We don't see any challenge on India-US trade deal negotiations," Agarwal told reporters while briefing on June 2023 trade data. He confirmed that an Indian team visited Washington in May and a U.S. team visited India in June.

The two governments announced "Mission 500" in February 2025, aiming to more than double bilateral trade to 500 billion by 2030. Trade flows have remained strong despite the tariff volatility, according to the Commerce Secretary.

Broader Trade Disruption

Brazil became the first country targeted under the new Section 301 strategy last week, facing 25% duties on furniture, ethanol, machinery, footwear, sugar, and other goods. The U.S. has also imposed a fresh 50% tariff on Canada under Section 338 of the Tariff Act.

The Trump administration has been rebuilding tariff pressure through multiple legal channels since the Supreme Court struck down its original emergency tariff authority. The new approach uses Section 301 investigations, which experts say have stronger legal footing but require more procedural steps, including public consultations and hearings.

For India, the coming days will test whether the positive diplomatic signals on the bilateral trade deal can withstand the broadening tariff offensive.
nri_angle: New tariffs could raise costs on Indian goods in the US and complicate the India-US trade deal that both governments say is ready to sign.
